title: Approaching the Inverse Neutron Scattering Problem with Neural Networks
authors: Jingyi Luo, Fletcher Williams, Ang-Kun Wu, David Dahlbom, Cristian D. Batista, Hao Zhang
abstract: Determining the microscopic Hamiltonian of a quantum magnet from inelastic neutron scattering measurements remains a central challenge in condensed matter physics. While the dynamical spin structure factor contains, in principle, sufficient information about the underlying interactions, extracting Hamiltonian parameters from experimental spectra constitutes a highly nontrivial inverse problem due to the large parameter space and the presence of experimental noise. Here we demonstrate that neural networks can efficiently solve this inverse problem for a broad class of quantum magnets. As a benchmark, we consider an eight-parameter family of honeycomb lattice Heisenberg spin models in the fully polarized phase, where the dynamical spin structure factor can be computed exactly within linear spin-wave theory. Using a large synthetic dataset of neutron scattering spectra, we train neural networks to infer the underlying Hamiltonian parameters directly from the dynamical response. We compare the performance of three different architectures---fully connected neural networks (FCNNs), one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNN1Ds), and two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNN2Ds)---and find that all achieve high predictive accuracy. Remarkably, the trained models remain robust in the presence of substantial experimental uncertainty, reliably recovering the Hamiltonian parameters even when the input spectra are contaminated by random noise with amplitudes reaching $10\%$ of the signal intensity. Our results establish machine learning as a powerful framework for quantitative Hamiltonian reconstruction from neutron scattering data and provide a practical route toward automated characterization of quantum magnetic materials.
summary: This paper tackles the difficult inverse problem of reconstructing a quantum magnet's Hamiltonian from neutron scattering data. By training neural networks on synthetic data generated from an exactly solvable honeycomb model, the authors show that ML provides a powerful, robust, and automated framework for quantitative Hamiltonian characterization. This offers a practical route for analyzing real-world quantum magnetic materials.
main_problem: The central challenge is determining the microscopic Hamiltonian of a quantum magnet from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements, which is a highly non-trivial inverse problem.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that neural networks can efficiently solve this inverse problem, achieving high predictive accuracy even when input spectra are contaminated by significant random noise.
method: They train neural networks (FCNN, CNN1D, CNN2D) on a large synthetic dataset generated by a forward solver that computes the dynamical spin structure factor from known Hamiltonian parameters.
model_or_system: The study focuses on an eight-parameter family of isotropic Heisenberg spin models on a honeycomb lattice, analyzed in the fully polarized phase using linear spin-wave theory.
key_observables: The dynamical spin structure factor, S(q, omega), which is the magnetic contribution to the neutron-scattering response.
important_parameters: The eight exchange couplings $\{J_1, \dots, J_8\}$ that define the Hamiltonian.
main_assumptions: The method relies on the availability of an accurate and efficient forward solver to construct the necessary training database, and the initial benchmark uses an exactly solvable model.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the workflow: Forward solver $ightarrow$ Train NN $ightarrow$ Deploy NN for inference. Figure 2(a) shows the honeycomb lattice structure and the bonds corresponding to the eight coupling constants.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the inverse problem, details the forward calculation using spin-wave theory for the specific model, proposes using NNs to map spectra back to parameters, and validates the approach using synthetic data and noise robustness tests.
why_interesting: While the focus is on condensed matter magnetism, the methodology—using ML to invert complex physical measurements—is highly relevant to characterizing quantum materials where direct theoretical calculation is intractable.

During deployment, the trained network infers the Hamiltonian parameters directly from neutron- scattering data.
